nodes.label: Theme Token Porting
nodes.rationale: @theme / @theme inline is Tailwind v4 syntax with no v3 equivalent, so under Nativewind v4 tokens must move into theme.extend in tailwind.config.js, which is what makes bg-primary and text-foreground resolve at all; under v5 the @theme block ports to the CSS entry unchanged.

nodes.label: Third-Party Component Class Mapping
nodes.rationale: Before passing className to a third-party component such as LinearGradient, check whether it forwards classes to a supported primitive or needs an explicit mapping (cssInterop in v4, a returned styled wrapper in v5); mappings are defined once outside render so the mapped component can be reused and probed.

nodes.label: Uniwind global.css Theme
nodes.rationale: Uniwind consumes Tailwind v4 so the mockup's classes carry over unchanged, and it resolves theme colors from global.css; the project's existing file structure is followed and :root tokens are ported into --color-* names in whatever shape that file actually uses.

nodes.label: withUniwind Third-Party Wrapping
nodes.rationale: Components from other libraries accept className once wrapped; wrapping each one once in its own file and importing the wrapped version everywhere keeps a single mapping instead of repeating withUniwind at every call site.

nodes.label: Nativewind Build Step Checklist
nodes.rationale: A missing build step presents as every class doing nothing at all, silently, so the per-major checklist (Babel preset, Metro wrapper, tailwind.config.js, PostCSS, CSS entry in the root layout) is checked before rewriting any class.

nodes.label: Nativewind Major Compatibility Matrix
nodes.rationale: The two Nativewind lines consume different Tailwind majors (v4 expects Tailwind v3, v5 expects Tailwind v4) and everything else branches on which one is installed, so the resolved version must be read from the lockfile before any styling decision.

nodes.label: Tailwind v4 to v3 Class Mapping
nodes.norm_label: tailwind v4 to v3 class mapping
nodes.rationale: A class that resolves to nothing is usually one of a known set of renames (shadow-xs, rounded-xs, outline-hidden, bg-linear-to-b, bg-(--token)); under Nativewind v5 none of the mapping applies, so the installed major decides whether renaming or a different mechanism is needed.

nodes.label: Root Font Size Units Alignment
nodes.rationale: Sleek's default web rem is 16px while Nativewind's native default is 14, so spacing and typography shrink on device despite matching on web; the root size must be aligned per major (inlineRem: 16 for v4, :root font-size for v5) rather than assumed to carry across.

nodes.label: Color Token Conversion to Native Parser
nodes.norm_label: color token conversion to native parser
nodes.rationale: React Native's color parser reads hex, rgb() and named colors and carries no oklch matcher, so a raw oklch(...) token resolves to nothing; converting each token once in the token module keeps every consumer correct instead of scattering conversions.

nodes.label: Density-Independent Pixel Unit Mapping
nodes.rationale: React Native styles use unitless numbers in density-independent pixels, so Tailwind's 0.25rem spacing steps and rem/em font sizes must be resolved against the HTML root font size; viewport-relative sizes go through useWindowDimensions() and then pass numeric native values.

nodes.label: Static StyleSheet Composition
nodes.rationale: One StyleSheet.create per component file holds everything static and conditional styling composes with arrays, while values that genuinely change per render (a measured width, an animated height) stay inline.

nodes.label: Uniwind OKLCH Token Support
nodes.rationale: Uniwind documents first-class OKLCH support, so oklch(...) values port across as-is instead of being converted to hex like other native styling paths require.

nodes.label: Native iOS Build and Submit Profiles
nodes.norm_label: native ios build and submit profiles
nodes.rationale: The actual shared scheme is selected and explicit build configurations are used, because developmentClient: true configures the Expo development client rather than generic Swift debugging; ascAppId is the numeric App Store Connect app ID, not the EAS project UUID, bundle ID or Apple team ID.

nodes.label: Minimal package.json for Native Projects
nodes.rationale: The package file is tooling metadata, not a JavaScript app: expo, react, react-native, index.js, Metro and expo-dev-client must not be added merely to use EAS, and a matching lockfile for the chosen package manager is kept.

nodes.label: Minimal Podfile Adapter
nodes.rationale: The default EAS iOS worker still runs pod install for checked-in native projects, so a minimal Podfile with the app's real deployment target and target name serves as an adapter without adding React Native pods; projects that must avoid CocoaPods use a custom EAS build instead.

nodes.label: EAS Build and Submit Command Surface
nodes.norm_label: eas build and submit command surface
nodes.rationale: Production builds, per-platform builds and --auto-submit cover the normal release path, while npx testflight is the Expo/React Native shortcut for iOS TestFlight.

nodes.label: eas.json Configuration for Builds and Submits
nodes.norm_label: eas.json configuration for builds and submits
nodes.rationale: eas init links or creates the EAS project and eas build:configure creates build profiles; existing project and store identifiers are preserved when a release setup already exists, and appVersionSource remote makes EAS the source of truth for version numbers.

nodes.label: EAS Hosting Deployment Workflow
nodes.rationale: npx expo export -p web ships the web bundle and any Expo Router API routes together, so a single eas deploy handles a full website, an API-routes-only backend, or both; --prod promotes a preview URL to production.

nodes.label: Development Client eas.json Profile
nodes.rationale: A development profile with developmentClient true bundles expo-dev-client for development builds, autoIncrement bumps build numbers and appVersionSource remote makes EAS the source of truth for version numbers.

nodes.label: EAS App Stores Agent Interface Descriptor
nodes.norm_label: eas app stores agent interface descriptor

nodes.label: Native Swift iOS Apps on EAS
nodes.norm_label: native swift ios apps on eas

nodes.label: Keep the Delivery Wrapper Small
nodes.rationale: Hand-maintained native code stays checked in and expo prebuild --clean is not a setup step for this path, because it would regenerate the native directories and destroy the project's source of truth.

nodes.label: Project Path Selection for Store Releases
nodes.norm_label: project path selection for store releases
nodes.rationale: The native iOS path keeps the Xcode project and Swift code as the app's source of truth, so the Expo/React Native quick-start and development-client examples are explicitly excluded from it; EAS is a delivery service and native apps can use it without adding Expo or React Native to their runtime.

nodes.label: Remote Version Management
nodes.rationale: EAS manages version numbers automatically via appVersionSource remote, but the remote counter alone does not prove Xcode used it, so the archived CFBundleVersion must be inspected when native iOS versioning is set up or changed.

nodes.label: Deferred Permission Gating
nodes.rationale: Permission prompts fire on user intent (first save, first record) behind an explanation screen instead of on mount, avoiding surprise system prompts.

nodes.label: Hook-Based Resource Management
nodes.rationale: expo-audio players and recorders are hook-managed, so resources are released on unmount and no explicit unloadAsync call is required.

nodes.label: Verified WCAG AA Contrast Rules
nodes.rationale: Contrast ratios were measured per token pair and the ratios are mandatory in mobile: normal text 4.5:1, large text 3:1. Lime and amber fail as small text on light backgrounds (2.62:1 / 2.09:1), so in light mode they are restricted to backgrounds, borders and large iconography; white text on lime is banned (2.76:1). Error red on dark and warning amber on light are demoted to borders/icons only, and the message body uses primary text on ink instead.

nodes.label: ARIA Tabs Pattern
nodes.rationale: Tabs require role=tablist/tab/tabpanel with aria-selected, aria-controls and roving tabindex, because arrow-key navigation and a single tab stop are what screen-reader users expect from a tab widget.

nodes.label: Dragging Movements Pattern
nodes.rationale: Any action triggered by dragging must offer a single-pointer alternative; the same rule extends to sliders, map panning and colour pickers.

nodes.label: Error Handling Pattern
nodes.rationale: Errors must be announced to screen readers with role="alert" and the first invalid field must receive focus on submit, so the user is not left hunting for which field failed.

nodes.label: Form Labels Pattern
nodes.rationale: Every input needs a programmatically associated label, either explicit (for/id) or implicit (wrapping label), plus optional instructions wired through aria-describedby.

nodes.label: Live Regions and Notifications Pattern
nodes.rationale: aria-live announces dynamic content without moving focus; polite waits for a pause in speech while assertive interrupts. The container must be cleared before writing so a repeated message still triggers a new announcement.

nodes.label: Modal Focus Trap Pattern
nodes.rationale: Tab and Shift+Tab must cycle inside the dialog and Escape must close it, otherwise keyboard users are trapped. The native <dialog> element already handles the trap, so it is preferred where browser support allows.

nodes.label: Skip Link Pattern
nodes.rationale: Lets keyboard users bypass repetitive navigation and jump straight to main content; the link is visually hidden off-canvas until focused.

nodes.label: Client-Side Data Fetching
nodes.rationale: Automatic deduplication and efficient data fetching patterns reduce redundant network requests.

nodes.label: useSWRSubscription
nodes.rationale: SWR subscription hook that keeps a single shared global listener alive for every component instance using the hook.

nodes.label: { passive: true } listener option
nodes.rationale: Declares that a listener will not call preventDefault() so the browser can scroll without waiting; correct for tracking, analytics and logging, wrong for custom swipe gestures, zoom controls or any listener that must cancel the default behaviour.

nodes.label: SWR (stale-while-revalidate)
nodes.rationale: Client data-fetching library providing request deduplication, caching and revalidation across component instances.

nodes.label: useImmutableSWR
nodes.rationale: Project-level hook for data that never changes, avoiding revalidation of static resources such as configuration.

nodes.label: useSWRMutation
nodes.rationale: Mutation hook whose trigger() performs a write and revalidates the affected keys instead of reading through useSWR.

nodes.label: SWR documentation
nodes.rationale: Reference for useSWR, useSWRMutation and the subscription APIs used by the client data-fetching rules.

nodes.label: Deduplicate Global Event Listeners
nodes.rationale: Each hook instance that registers its own window listener multiplies listeners across the tree; a module-level callback registry plus one shared subscription collapses N instances into a single listener.

nodes.label: Use Passive Event Listeners for Scrolling Performance
nodes.norm_label: use passive event listeners for scrolling performance
nodes.rationale: Browsers wait for touch and wheel listeners to finish before checking preventDefault(), which delays scrolling; passive listeners enable immediate scrolling but must not be used for listeners that need to prevent the default action.

nodes.label: Use SWR for Automatic Deduplication
nodes.rationale: Plain useEffect + fetch makes every component instance issue its own request; SWR shares one in-flight request across instances and adds caching and revalidation.

nodes.label: Advanced Patterns
nodes.rationale: Advanced patterns for specific cases that require careful implementation.

nodes.label: Stale Closure
nodes.rationale: Callbacks capture the props and state of the render that created them, so they keep reading outdated values after state changes unless the callback identity or the update form is made stable.

nodes.label: useEffectEvent (React hook)
nodes.rationale: Returns a stable function identity that always invokes the latest version of the wrapped handler, so effects can read fresh values without listing them as dependencies.

nodes.label: Do Not Put Effect Events in Dependency Arrays
nodes.norm_label: do not put effect events in dependency arrays
nodes.rationale: Effect Event functions intentionally get a new identity on every render, so listing one in a useEffect dependency array makes the effect re-run every render and trips the React Hooks lint rule; depend on the reactive values and call the Effect Event from inside the effect body or its subscriptions.

nodes.label: Store Event Handlers in Refs
nodes.rationale: Callbacks held in a ref keep the effect subscription stable, so the listener is not torn down and re-registered every time the callback identity changes.

nodes.label: Initialize App Once, Not Per Mount
nodes.norm_label: initialize app once, not per mount
nodes.rationale: Components remount and their effects re-run, so app-wide initialization placed in useEffect([]) runs twice in development and again on every remount; a module-level guard makes it run once per app load.

nodes.label: useEffectEvent for Stable Callback Refs
nodes.rationale: Accessing the latest values inside callbacks without adding them to dependency arrays prevents effect re-runs while avoiding stale closures.

nodes.label: Conditional Workflow Jobs
nodes.rationale: A run-type job can compute a change flag and expose it through GITHUB_OUTPUT so a later build job's if condition skips unnecessary builds.

nodes.label: PR Previews with EAS Update
nodes.rationale: OTA updates are deployed for pull requests through an update-type job keyed to a per-PR branch name, letting a change be exercised on a device before it reaches the store.

nodes.label: Production Release Workflow
nodes.rationale: The release workflow builds both platforms from a version tag and chains each submit job to its own build via needs, so a submission can only run against an artifact that was actually produced.

nodes.label: Workflow Expression Contexts
nodes.rationale: Dynamic values use ${{ }} syntax over defined contexts — github, inputs, needs, jobs, steps and workflow — so expressions must reference valid contexts and outputs.

nodes.label: Workflow File Location and Size Limit
nodes.norm_label: workflow file location and size limit

nodes.label: Workflow Top-Level Structure
nodes.rationale: A workflow file has name, on, jobs, defaults and concurrency top-level keys, with at least one trigger and a jobs map required.

nodes.label: Live Workflow Schema Fetch
nodes.rationale: The JSON schema and syntax documentation are fetched before generating or editing a workflow because these resources evolve as new features are added and memorized values go stale; the EAS CLI remains the authoritative final validator.

nodes.label: workflow:validate Command
nodes.rationale: Validation runs through eas-cli workflow:validate per changed file until it prints that the configuration is valid, because unlike schema-only validation it also checks build profile references against eas.json and performs EAS server-side validation; a local YAML or JSON Schema validator is not a substitute.

nodes.label: Semantic Color Tokens (Light and Dark Modes)
nodes.norm_label: semantic color tokens (light and dark modes)

nodes.label: Sleek API Error Shapes and Run-Level Errors
nodes.norm_label: sleek api error shapes and run-level errors

nodes.label: Implementing Sleek Designs in React Native / Expo
nodes.norm_label: implementing sleek designs in react native / expo

nodes.label: Native Design Token Mapping Instruction for Mobile AI
nodes.norm_label: native design token mapping instruction for mobile ai
nodes.rationale: The palette and type tables are meant to be replicated verbatim as native design tokens (Color.kt, AppColors.dart, CSS variables) rather than re-invented, because FrontEnd/src/index.css is the single source of truth and new hex values are forbidden.

nodes.label: Chat Run Polling Protocol
nodes.rationale: Runs are async: poll from 2s and back off to 5s after 10s, for up to 10 minutes, exiting only on completed or failed. Elapsed time does not prove completion and does not release the project run lock, so a new attempt must not start while the previous outcome is unknown.

nodes.label: One Active Run per Project
nodes.rationale: Keep one active run per project and follow a known run to a terminal status before sending the next message. A 409 carries no active-run pointer and the API has no run-list endpoint, so an unknown run ID must be reported rather than invented.

nodes.label: Safe Retries with Idempotency Keys
nodes.rationale: Choose an idempotency-key before sending so a lost response can be replayed with the same payload and key to recover the original run. After request_message_persist_failed or after the user resolves out_of_credits, a new logical attempt needs a new key.

nodes.label: Screenshot Review Loop
nodes.rationale: After every run producing screen_created or screen_updated operations, take screenshots and show them to the user. The phone-shaped user shot is the right framing for showing a screen but the wrong one for judging it, because everything below the fold is cropped away; use the full-height review shot for self-review and check the component HTML before reporting content as missing.

nodes.label: Authoring a Style Direction
nodes.rationale: A style direction is a single comprehensive paragraph covering mood, color strategy, typography feel, layout philosophy, component style, imagery and one or two distinctive details; anything that only sets a mood reads as a hint rather than a direction. Personality belongs in color, type and imagery rather than unusual layout or navigation, and a style direction must not be combined with a referenceId because the reference already carries a full style guide.

nodes.label: Build the Feature, Not the Mockup
nodes.norm_label: build the feature, not the mockup
nodes.rationale: A mockup shipped verbatim is a convincing dead app: structure, layout and styling are the spec, but names, numbers and copy are placeholders that must be replaced by real state, props or API data. A mockup also shows only one moment, so empty, single-item, loading and error states must be decided separately.

nodes.label: Design Token Porting
nodes.rationale: The project theme is inlined into every screen, so it is ported once into a single token module that every component reads from. --radius is a base that must be resolved with calc() into concrete numbers, --shape must be tested by value rather than presence because React Native has no corner-shape, and unsupported colour formats are converted once while supported ones are preserved.

nodes.label: Flex Direction Row/Column Trap
nodes.rationale: Sleek writes the web idiom where display:flex is a row, but React Native defaults flexDirection to column, so a horizontal row silently renders as a vertical stack. Every flex in the source must be given an explicit direction; flex-1 maps to flex:1 and inline-flex is dropped with a value warning.

nodes.label: Font Porting from Theme Families
nodes.rationale: The head link tags give font families, not the weights used; the real weights live in the body's font-* Tailwind classes, so only those faces are bundled. An exported alias like --font-font-heading does not define the font-heading utility, so malformed aliases are corrected when porting and any remaining discrepancy with the screenshot is recorded rather than silently resolved.

nodes.label: Iconify Icon Porting
nodes.rationale: Use the exact icon set and name found in the HTML because matching icons carry design fidelity. On Expo the mdi:* prefix is a free rename to MaterialCommunityIcons; other prefixes go through the Iconify SVG API and are rendered with react-native-svg's SvgXml so no extra native dependency is needed.

nodes.label: Infer the Route Tree from the Screen Set
nodes.norm_label: infer the route tree from the screen set
nodes.rationale: Each Sleek screen is a standalone document that redraws the whole chrome, so the screen set must be read as one app and the navigator inferred before implementing: a repeated bottom bar means tab siblings, a back arrow means a Stack child, a hamburger means a Drawer, and horizontal tabs or a FAB are components rather than routes. The navigator owns the chrome and draws it once.

nodes.label: Safe Area Insets
nodes.rationale: The mockup renders edge to edge with no notch, status bar or home indicator, so an unguarded screen draws under the system bars; Expo SDK 54+ makes Android edge-to-edge the default. Insets come from react-native-safe-area-context rather than React Native's own SafeAreaView, which only insets on iOS, and each edge is inset exactly once.

nodes.label: Cross-Platform Shadows
nodes.rationale: boxShadow maps the mockup's CSS shadow 1:1 on both platforms and is the default choice because React Native only ships the New Architecture from 0.82. Legacy projects must set iOS shadowColor/shadowOffset/shadowOpacity/shadowRadius plus Android elevation and a backgroundColor, accepting that Android only approximates the exact shadow.

nodes.label: Strings Must Live Inside <Text>
nodes.rationale: Every string must be rendered inside <Text>, including strings hidden in && branches, ternaries or stray {' '}. A bare string under a <View> fails silently: the New Architecture routes the warning through console.error, so in a production build the string simply disappears and nothing throws.

nodes.label: Which Version to Use
nodes.rationale: activeVersion is nullable, so default to the versions entry whose version equals activeVersion and fall back to the highest numeric version; the selected entry's id must also be passed in componentVersionOverrides because the renderer can otherwise produce an empty frame. If there are no versions at all, stop and report that there is no code to implement.

nodes.label: @expo/ui Over React Native Controls
nodes.rationale: @expo/ui renders native SwiftUI / Jetpack Compose pickers and follow platform conventions automatically, so it is recommended over the React Native control fallbacks.

nodes.label: Prefer @expo/ui Components
nodes.rationale: @expo/ui renders real SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose with platform design conventions and works in Expo Go, so it is checked before React Native built-ins or community libraries.

nodes.label: New Architecture Requirement
nodes.rationale: CSS gradients depend on the Fabric renderer of the New Architecture, so they are unavailable in the old architecture and inside Expo Go.

nodes.label: JavaScript Performance
nodes.rationale: Micro-optimizations for hot paths can add up to meaningful improvements.

nodes.label: Module-Level Memoization Cache
nodes.rationale: A Map keyed by the function inputs that lives outside React, so the same computation is not repeated for identical arguments and the cache is invalidated explicitly when the underlying data changes.

nodes.label: Loop-Invariant Lookup Hoisting
nodes.rationale: Reading the same unchanged property on every iteration repeats the lookup; computing it once before the loop removes the repeated work, and caching the array length likewise avoids a per-iteration bounds read.

nodes.label: How we made the Vercel Dashboard twice as fast (Vercel engineering blog)
nodes.norm_label: how we made the vercel dashboard twice as fast (vercel engineering blog)
nodes.rationale: Case study showing how module-level caching of repeated function results was used to speed up the dashboard.

nodes.label: Cache Repeated Function Calls
nodes.rationale: Memoizing pure helper calls with a module-level Map removes redundant computation in hot render paths; a Map rather than a hook keeps the cache usable from utilities and event handlers, not just React components.

nodes.label: Cache Property Access in Loops
nodes.rationale: Hoisting an invariant property lookup out of the loop body turns three lookups per iteration into one, which matters when the loop runs on every render.

nodes.label: Assertion Functions
nodes.rationale: An assertion function (`asserts value is string`) narrows the value in the caller after it returns, but it throws at runtime, so it must only be used behind a genuine check rather than as a cast.

nodes.label: Builder Pattern with Type Safety
nodes.rationale: Accumulating state in the type parameter (S) makes build() callable only once all required keys are set, moving completeness checking from runtime validation to the type system.

nodes.label: Deep Readonly and Deep Partial
nodes.rationale: A recursive mapped type propagates readonly/optional modifiers into nested objects and arrays, which the shallow built-in Readonly and Partial utilities cannot do.

nodes.label: Type Guards
nodes.rationale: A guard narrows an unknown value at runtime so downstream code can use the concrete type without assertions; composing a guard with a per-item guard (isArrayOf) narrows whole collections at once.

nodes.label: Type-Safe API Client
nodes.rationale: Encoding endpoint, method, params, body and response in a single configuration type lets the compiler derive the request argument shape and the return type, so a malformed call fails at compile time instead of producing an unchecked network request.

nodes.label: Type-Safe Form Validation
nodes.rationale: Encoding per-field validation rules in a mapped type yields a typed error map (string[] per field) returned as null when valid, so validation messages stay aligned with the form's own data shape.

nodes.label: Type-Safe Event Emitter
nodes.rationale: Typing listeners as a mapped type over the event map gives each event its own payload type, so emitting 'user:created' without the required 'name' field becomes a compile-time error rather than an undefined access at runtime.

nodes.label: Open Issues to Investigate
nodes.rationale: Three problems are still open: navigation is slow to open and the cause is unknown, loading screens and validation messages are missing, and styled-components cannot be used.

nodes.label: TypeScript Advanced Types - Detailed Worked Examples
nodes.norm_label: typescript advanced types - detailed worked examples

nodes.label: Native Action Bridge via Async Props
nodes.norm_label: native action bridge via async props
nodes.rationale: Native capabilities are exposed to the webview by passing async functions as props, which keeps the native/web boundary declarative and avoids global state.

nodes.label: Isolated Webview Context
nodes.rationale: A DOM component runs in its own JavaScript context inside the webview, so state cannot be shared directly with native code; the boundary must stay explicit and serializable.

nodes.label: Player/View Separation
nodes.rationale: Decoupling player logic from the view lets one player be shared by several views and preloaded without mounting a VideoView.

nodes.label: Deprecated Package Migration
nodes.rationale: Code usage is migrated before the old package is removed so the app never references a module that no longer exists.

nodes.label: Locked Tested Version Set
nodes.rationale: The react-native-wgpu, three and @react-three/fiber versions are tested together; mismatched versions cause type errors and runtime issues.

nodes.label: Use Transitions for Non-Urgent Updates
nodes.rationale: Frequent, non-urgent state updates such as scroll position block the UI on every event. Marking them as transitions lets React keep the interface responsive while the update is scheduled.

nodes.label: Use useDeferredValue for Expensive Derived Renders
nodes.norm_label: use usedeferredvalue for expensive derived renders
nodes.rationale: The deferred value lags behind the input so React can prioritize the urgent input update and render the expensive result when idle, keeping the input responsive during heavy filtering or visualization work. The expensive computation must also be wrapped in useMemo keyed on the deferred value.

nodes.label: Use useRef for Transient Values
nodes.rationale: Values that change frequently but do not affect what is displayed (mouse trackers, intervals, transient flags) belong in useRef: updating a ref does not trigger a re-render, while component state should be reserved for UI state.

nodes.label: Parallel Data Fetching with Component Composition
nodes.norm_label: parallel data fetching with component composition
nodes.rationale: React Server Components execute sequentially within a tree, so a sibling component's await blocks its siblings. Restructuring the tree with composition (or a children prop) lets each component fetch in parallel and eliminates server-side waterfalls.

nodes.label: Parallel Nested Data Fetching
nodes.rationale: Awaiting a batch of parent fetches and then a second batch of nested fetches makes one slow item block all nested fetches. Chaining each dependent fetch inside its own item promise lets the remaining items progress independently.

nodes.label: Discriminated Unions
nodes.rationale: A literal discriminator field (status or type) lets the compiler narrow union members, replacing runtime type checks with exhaustive switch narrowing of async state machines and request lifecycles.

nodes.label: Common TypeScript Pitfalls
nodes.rationale: Over-using any and ignoring strict null checks defeat the purpose of TypeScript and cause runtime errors, while skipping discriminated unions forfeits narrowing and forgetting readonly modifiers permits unintended mutations; overly complex types also slow compilation and circular references break it outright.

nodes.label: Hosting Environment Secrets
nodes.rationale: Server-side secrets are read from process.env and provisioned with eas env:create per environment or through the Expo dashboard, keeping API keys out of the client bundle.

nodes.label: Route-Level Data Loaders
nodes.rationale: Loaders are async functions exported from route files that load data before the route renders, following the Remix/React Router loader model. One function is written and the framework manages execution: server-side during initial SSR page load with JSON embedded in the HTML, and over HTTP on client-side navigation.

nodes.label: LoaderFunction Type and Params
nodes.rationale: Loaders with params use LoaderFunction<T> from expo-server; the first argument is an immutable request-like object (undefined in static mode) and the second holds path parameters only, with query parameters read from new URL(request.url).searchParams.

nodes.label: StatusError and setResponseHeaders
nodes.rationale: StatusError from expo-server produces HTTP error responses from a loader and setResponseHeaders sets cache-control or similar headers, both supplied by expo-server which is already a dependency of expo-router.

nodes.label: Suspense and ErrorBoundary Boundaries
nodes.rationale: useLoaderData suspends during client-side navigation, so the hook is pushed into a child component wrapped in Suspense; the boundary must sit above the component calling useLoaderData, and the nearest ErrorBoundary catches thrown StatusError values.

nodes.label: AbortController Cancellation on Unmount
nodes.rationale: A controller created in the effect and aborted in the cleanup cancels the in-flight request on unmount, and the AbortError is swallowed so an intentional cancellation is not reported as a failure; React Query performs this cancellation automatically.

nodes.label: React Query onlineManager Sync
nodes.rationale: Syncing React Query's onlineManager with NetInfo lets queries pause while offline and resume when connectivity returns, giving offline-first behavior without bespoke caching code.

nodes.label: ApiError Typed Error Handling
nodes.rationale: HTTP failures are surfaced as a typed ApiError carrying status and code, while transport failures are normalized to a NETWORK_ERROR with status 0, so callers can distinguish an API refusal from a connectivity failure.

nodes.label: Auth Token Management and Refresh
nodes.rationale: Tokens live in expo-secure-store rather than AsyncStorage, and refresh uses a single in-flight promise guarded by an isRefreshing flag so concurrent callers share one refresh instead of stampeding the auth endpoint.

nodes.label: Typed Fetch Wrapper
nodes.rationale: The response status must be checked before parsing, and axios is avoided in favour of expo/fetch so platform-specific networking behavior is preserved.

nodes.label: Networking Decision Tree
nodes.rationale: A routing decision tree maps each networking need (route-level loading, basic fetch, caching, authentication, error handling, offline, environment config, performance) to a specific technique so the approach is chosen deliberately rather than by default.

nodes.label: React Query (TanStack Query) Setup
nodes.rationale: React Query is chosen for complex caching and state management while simpler needs use SWR or custom hooks; a QueryClientProvider with a staleTime and retry policy is mounted in the root layout, and mutations invalidate and refetch affected query keys.

nodes.label: Cache Invalidation Flow
nodes.rationale: The typical flow closes the loop between the three hooks: useQuery fetches and caches, useMutation sends the modification, and useQueryClient's invalidateQueries marks the cache stale so useQuery refetches automatically.

nodes.label: Optimistic Updates (onMutate)
nodes.rationale: onMutate fires before the request is sent, so the UI updates instantly and reverts if the server rejects the change; this is the only supported optimistic-update path because useQuery has no equivalent.

nodes.label: Key Query Options (queryKey, enabled, staleTime, refetchInterval, select, placeholderData)
nodes.norm_label: key query options (querykey, enabled, staletime, refetchinterval, select, placeholderdata)

nodes.label: QueryClient
nodes.rationale: QueryClient is the central server-state manager and cache engine: it owns cache storage and organisation, the data lifecycle (refetch on reconnect/focus/interval, retry handling, garbage collection) and UI synchronisation without prop drilling.

nodes.label: queryKey
nodes.rationale: queryKey is the unique cache identifier: the same key means the same cache entry, which is what makes deduplicated fetching and targeted invalidation possible.

nodes.label: useMutation
nodes.rationale: useMutation is the imperative write hook: it wraps an async mutationFn and runs it on demand through mutate()/mutateAsync(), does not share cached results between instances and does not retry by default, so a write must be followed by an explicit cache invalidation for readers to see the new state.

nodes.label: useQuery
nodes.rationale: useQuery is the declarative read hook: it runs queryFn on mount without useEffect or useState, caches the result by queryKey so a second component asking for the same key does not refetch, and exposes isPending/isError/isFetching/isStale/data/refetch plus 3 retries with exponential backoff by default.

nodes.label: useQueryClient
nodes.rationale: useQueryClient exposes programmatic access to the cache (getQueryData, setQueryData, invalidateQueries) so any part of the application can force a refresh without prop drilling.

nodes.label: Expo Data Fetching Agent Interface Descriptor
nodes.norm_label: expo data fetching agent interface descriptor

nodes.label: Offline Support and Request Cancellation Reference
nodes.norm_label: offline support and request cancellation reference

nodes.label: Loader Server-Side Secrets
nodes.rationale: Loaders run on the server and can read secrets and session cookies directly, so non-prefixed process.env variables are used there rather than EXPO_PUBLIC_ ones which are embedded in the client bundle.

nodes.label: Server versus Static Web Output
nodes.rationale: Server output runs the loader on every request with full request access and suits frequently changing or personalized content, while static output runs it at build time and suits content that is the same for all users; both require unstable_useServerDataLoaders and only server mode requires unstable_useServerRendering.

nodes.label: EXPO_PUBLIC_ Environment Variables
nodes.rationale: Only EXPO_PUBLIC_-prefixed variables reach the client bundle and they are inlined at build time, not runtime, so secrets must never use that prefix; server-side secrets in API routes use non-prefixed variables, and the dev server must be restarted after changing .env files.

nodes.label: Four Screen States (Loading, Error, Empty, Content)
nodes.norm_label: four screen states (loading, error, empty, content)
nodes.rationale: Loading is not empty: empty means resolved with zero items, not missing data, and in TanStack Query v5 a disabled or offline-paused query can have no data without being loading. Refetches keep stale content with a nonblocking error, and initial UI or redirects are gated on hydration to avoid flashing the wrong screen on cold start.

nodes.label: Saves Preserve Work
nodes.rationale: While a mutation is pending repeat submission is disabled; on failure the draft is retained, an inline error is shown and the user can retry, and the draft is cleared only after success. Optimistic updates must restore the previous value or mark the edit unsynced on failure.

nodes.label: SecureStore over AsyncStorage
nodes.rationale: Storing tokens in AsyncStorage is explicitly marked wrong because it is not secure; SecureStore is the correct home for sensitive data.

nodes.label: TypeScript Performance Considerations
nodes.rationale: Deeply nested conditional types and unbounded recursive types slow the compiler, so complex type computations must be cached, recursion depth limited, and simple types preferred.

nodes.label: TypeScript Best Practices
nodes.rationale: Prefer unknown over any to keep type checking enforceable, interface for object shapes because it yields better error messages, type for unions and complex types, type guards instead of type assertions, const assertions to preserve literal types, strict compiler options, and JSDoc on complex types so intent survives the compiler.

nodes.label: iOS Credential Setup
nodes.rationale: An App Store Connect API key is recommended because it avoids 2FA prompts in CI/CD; Apple ID with an app-specific password is the manual alternative, and private key material is kept outside version control.

nodes.label: iOS Version and Build Numbers
nodes.rationale: CFBundleShortVersionString is the user-facing version while CFBundleVersion is internal and must increment for every upload; with autoIncrement and remote versioning EAS increments its counter and writes native version metadata during the build, but the archive's CFBundleVersion must still be verified.

nodes.label: Google Play App Signing
nodes.rationale: EAS uses Google Play App Signing by default: the first upload creates an upload key, Play Store manages and re-signs with the signing key, and the upload key can be reset if compromised.

nodes.label: Google Play Release Tracks
nodes.rationale: internal (up to 100 testers), alpha (closed testing), beta (open testing) and production (public release) form the staged rollout ladder; the default eas submit creates the first release on the internal track.

nodes.label: Google Play Service Account Setup
nodes.rationale: A service account key path in eas.json (or a base64 environment variable or EAS secret) authenticates automated submissions; the key must be kept out of version control and granted release permissions in Play Console.

nodes.label: Staged Rollout and Release Status
nodes.rationale: releaseStatus selects completed, draft, halted or inProgress, and inProgress with a rollout percentage releases to a slice of users, to be increased via Play Console or subsequent submissions.

nodes.label: Android versionCode Management
nodes.rationale: Android requires an incremented versionCode for each upload; autoIncrement with appVersionSource remote lets EAS track version codes automatically, and new apps must ship an AAB rather than an APK.

nodes.label: Explicit Info.plist Version Ownership
nodes.rationale: A generated plist with a fixed CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION can leave every archive reporting build 1 while the EAS dashboard shows increasing numbers, so an explicit INFOPLIST_FILE with GENERATE_INFOPLIST_FILE = NO is the tested approach; changing only app.json or observing an incremented remote counter is insufficient evidence.

nodes.label: AppIcon Alpha Channel Check
nodes.rationale: The default (Any/light) 1024px AppIcon PNG must have no alpha channel even if every pixel looks opaque, because an all-opaque RGBA file can still be rejected; transparency is preserved in dark variants and Icon Composer layers.

nodes.label: Native iOS Path Verification Scope
nodes.rationale: The approach was exercised with a SwiftUI app on EAS CLI 18.6.0 and Xcode 26.2, so worker/CLI behavior must be rechecked when tooling changes because project layout, custom hooks, extensions and signing requirements can differ.

nodes.label: eas submit:retry Eligibility
nodes.rationale: Retry eligibility is checked with submit:view and the cause diagnosed first, because retrying an unchanged archive cannot fix its build number or icon; retry is used only when repeating the existing authorized upload is appropriate.

nodes.label: TestFlight Troubleshooting Matrix
nodes.rationale: Account-level failures (missing agreement, app missing in App Store Connect, rejected optional release-notes parameter) cannot be fixed by retrying or rebuilding; artifact-level failures (duplicate build number, invalid icon alpha channel) require a corrected build and a new exact-ID submission.

nodes.label: Google Play Submission Monitoring
nodes.rationale: eas submit:list and eas submit:view report EAS submission jobs on CLI 23.2.0, but submit:status reads Apple status only, so an EAS job's success must not be treated as confirmation of a Play Console rollout.

nodes.label: EAS CLI Version Gating for Submission Commands
nodes.norm_label: eas cli version gating for submission commands
nodes.rationale: submit:list, submit:view and submit:status were verified with EAS CLI 23.2.0 while older CLIs such as 18.6.0 lack them, so the CLI version is checked first and a pinned npx eas-cli@23.2.0 invocation is preferred over importing internal Node modules or writing private GraphQL queries.

nodes.label: TestFlight Release State Tracking
nodes.rationale: Each verified state establishes only a limited claim — build finished, submission queued, Apple upload/processing succeeded, build available to testers, App Review approved and released — and the furthest state actually verified must be reported rather than treating --no-wait success as a finished upload.

nodes.label: Release State Verification Discipline
nodes.rationale: A successful EAS build or a queued submission does not establish Apple acceptance, tester access, or an App Store release; the exact build ID/version and the furthest verified release state must be reported instead.

nodes.label: Glass Availability Guards
nodes.rationale: Both isLiquidGlassAvailable() and isGlassEffectAPIAvailable() must be checked because some iOS 26 betas expose the OS but not the API and crash without the second guard.

nodes.label: Reduce Transparency Handling
nodes.rationale: When Reduce Transparency is enabled the glass and blur surfaces are replaced by a solid system background so content stays legible.

nodes.label: Defer Non-Critical Work with requestIdleCallback
nodes.rationale: requestIdleCallback schedules non-critical work during browser idle periods, keeping the main thread free for user interaction and animation, which reduces jank and improves perceived performance.

nodes.label: Use useTransition Over Manual Loading States
nodes.norm_label: use usetransition over manual loading states
nodes.rationale: useTransition provides a built-in isPending state, resets correctly even if the transition throws, keeps the UI responsive and lets new transitions cancel pending ones, replacing manual isLoading state that adds re-renders.

nodes.label: Expo Router API Routes (+api.ts)
nodes.rationale: API routes live in the app directory with a +api.ts suffix and export named functions per HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS), with dynamic segments exposing path params and catch-all routes exposing a slug array.

nodes.label: API Route Authentication Middleware
nodes.rationale: A shared requireAuth helper extracts the bearer token from the Authorization header and throws a 401 Response, so protected routes share one token-verification path rather than repeating it.

nodes.label: Edge Database Options
nodes.rationale: Because the filesystem is unavailable, storage must be a cloud database: Cloudflare D1, Turso, PlanetScale, Supabase or Neon, each reached over its HTTP/REST client.

nodes.label: When to Use (and Avoid) API Routes
nodes.norm_label: when to use (and avoid) api routes
nodes.rationale: API routes exist for server-side secrets, database operations, third-party API proxies, server-side validation, webhook endpoints, rate limiting and heavy computation; they are avoided when data is already public, no secrets are required, real-time updates are needed, the case is simple CRUD, uploads are involved, or authentication is the only concern.

nodes.label: Cloudflare Workers Runtime Limits
nodes.rationale: API routes run on Cloudflare Workers, so there is no Node.js filesystem, no native Node modules, a 30 second CPU timeout and no persistent connections (WebSockets need Durable Objects); Web APIs such as crypto.subtle, fetch, Request and Response replace Node equivalents.

nodes.label: API Route Rules
nodes.rationale: Never expose API keys or secrets in client code, always validate and sanitize user input, use proper HTTP status codes, handle errors gracefully with try/catch, keep one responsibility per endpoint, use TypeScript, and log errors server-side for debugging.

nodes.label: localStorage Polyfill
nodes.rationale: AsyncStorage was removed from React Native, so the expo-sqlite localStorage polyfill provides the familiar key-value API without an extra dependency.

nodes.label: Layout Thrashing (forced synchronous reflow)
nodes.rationale: Reading offsetWidth, offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect or getComputedStyle between style writes invalidates layout and forces the browser to recalculate synchronously, blocking the main thread.

nodes.label: CSS Triggers
nodes.rationale: Reference catalog of which CSS property changes force layout, used to identify layout-forcing operations.

nodes.label: Layout thrashing gist (Paul Irish)
nodes.rationale: Classic write/read interleaving example demonstrating how to batch DOM reads and writes.

nodes.label: Avoid Layout Thrashing
nodes.rationale: Interleaving style writes with layout reads forces a synchronous reflow on every read; batching all writes before the read (or all reads before the writes) limits the browser to a single recalculation, and CSS classes are preferred over inline styles because stylesheets are cached by the browser.

nodes.label: React DOM Resource Preloading APIs Reference
nodes.norm_label: react dom resource preloading apis reference

nodes.label: Use React DOM Resource Hints
nodes.rationale: React DOM resource hint APIs let the browser start fetching resources the page will need, especially in server components where loading can begin before the client receives the HTML, reducing load time for critical resources.

nodes.label: Structured Data Validation
nodes.rationale: The examples are starting points only: required and recommended properties must be verified against maintained Google Search and Schema.org documentation, and both the Rich Results Test and the Schema.org Validator are used because syntax validity alone does not imply rich-result eligibility.

nodes.label: Type Testing (AssertEqual / ExpectError)
nodes.rationale: Type-level assertions such as AssertEqual and the ExpectError helper let the compiler itself verify type behaviour, so a type regression fails the build instead of surfacing later as a runtime bug.

nodes.label: Submit an Identified Build to TestFlight
nodes.norm_label: submit an identified build to testflight
nodes.rationale: The source revision and returned build ID are recorded so the exact artifact can be submitted; for separate jobs the explicit build ID is passed rather than selecting whichever unrelated build is newest, and repeated noninteractive retries cannot complete first-time credential setup.

nodes.label: Local Development Client Builds
nodes.rationale: Building locally with --local is free while cloud builds consume EAS plan minutes; local output is an .ipa on iOS and an .apk or .aab on Android.

nodes.label: When Development Clients Are Needed
nodes.rationale: Expo Go is a playground for learning and quick experiments with the native libraries it bundles; most apps outgrow it and move to a development client, which is the recommended setup for any real or production app.

nodes.label: Four-State Data Loading
nodes.rationale: Every data-loading screen has explicit loading, error, empty and content states; showing the empty state while the first load is still resolving misleads the user.

nodes.label: ref as a Prop / forwardRef Removal
nodes.norm_label: ref as a prop / forwardref removal
nodes.rationale: React 19 passes ref as an ordinary prop, so the forwardRef wrapper and its extra typing are unnecessary overhead.

nodes.label: Security Checklist (parameterized queries, hashing, rate limiting, secrets)
nodes.norm_label: security checklist (parameterized queries, hashing, rate limiting, secrets)

nodes.label: Prevent Hydration Mismatch Without Flickering
nodes.rationale: Content that depends on client-side storage (localStorage, cookies) either breaks SSR or flashes after hydration; a synchronous inline script updates the DOM before React hydrates, avoiding both failure modes.

nodes.label: Synchronous Inline Theme Script
nodes.rationale: The inline script executes synchronously before the element is shown, so the DOM already carries the correct value and no flicker or hydration mismatch occurs; the pattern suits theme toggles, user preferences and authentication state.

nodes.label: Suppress Expected Hydration Mismatches
nodes.rationale: Some values are intentionally different on server and client (random IDs, dates, locale/timezone formatting); suppressHydrationWarning silences the noise for those expected differences, but must not be used to hide real bugs and should not be overused.

nodes.label: You Might Not Need an Effect
nodes.norm_label: you might not need an effect

nodes.label: Narrow Effect Dependencies
nodes.rationale: Depending on whole objects re-runs the effect on any field change; depending on primitives (or on a derived boolean) minimizes effect re-runs and only reacts to real transitions.

nodes.label: Calculate Derived State During Rendering
nodes.rationale: A value computable from current props/state should be derived during render instead of stored in state and updated in an effect, which otherwise causes extra renders and state drift; derived values or keyed resets are preferred over setState in effects.

nodes.label: Should this code move to an event handler? (react.dev removing-effect-dependencies)
nodes.norm_label: should this code move to an event handler? (react.dev removing-effect-dependencies)

nodes.label: Put Interaction Logic in Event Handlers
nodes.norm_label: put interaction logic in event handlers
nodes.rationale: A side effect caused by a specific user action should run in that action's handler. Modeling the action as state plus an effect makes the effect re-run on unrelated dependency changes and can duplicate the side effect.

nodes.label: Authenticate Server Actions Like API Routes
nodes.norm_label: authenticate server actions like api routes
nodes.rationale: Server Actions are exposed as public endpoints and can be invoked directly, so authentication, authorization and input validation must happen inside each action rather than relying on middleware, layout guards or page-level checks.

nodes.label: Reference-Based Serialization Deduplication
nodes.rationale: The same object reference is serialized once and reused; a new reference is serialized again. Deduplication recurses, so primitive arrays are fully duplicated while nested objects inside object arrays are deduplicated by reference.

nodes.label: Avoid Duplicate Serialization in RSC Props
nodes.norm_label: avoid duplicate serialization in rsc props
nodes.rationale: RSC to client serialization deduplicates by object reference rather than value, so transformations that create new references (.toSorted, .filter, .map, .slice, spread) duplicate the payload. Transforming on the client keeps the wire size minimal.

nodes.label: Minimize Serialization at RSC Boundaries
nodes.rationale: The React Server/Client boundary serializes every object property into strings embedded in the HTML response, so payload size directly drives page weight and load time. Passing only the fields the client actually uses keeps the boundary minimal.

nodes.label: Deprecated Import Check
nodes.rationale: A rewritten import can still be a deprecated re-export shim, so each rewritten symbol is resolved to its source and checked for a @deprecated tag before the change is mass-applied.

nodes.label: Stack Import Caveat
nodes.rationale: The root Stack export is the Expo Router layout component used in route files, so it must never be rewritten to expo-router/js-stack.

nodes.label: Barrel File
nodes.rationale: An entry point that re-exports multiple modules (e.g. index.js doing export * from './module'); the pattern defeats tree-shaking when the library is external and slows builds substantially when it is bundled.

nodes.label: lucide-react
nodes.rationale: Icon library whose entry file re-exports thousands of modules; importing the barrel loads 1,583 modules (~2.8s extra in dev) and it ships no .d.ts for deep import paths, so optimizePackageImports is the safe fix.

nodes.label: @mui/material
nodes.rationale: Component library whose barrel entry loads 2,225 modules (~4.2s extra in dev); deep imports such as @mui/material/Button load only what is used.

nodes.label: Next.js optimizePackageImports
nodes.rationale: Build-time config that rewrites barrel imports into direct imports, keeping TypeScript type safety and editor autocompletion while eliminating the barrel import cost.

nodes.label: How we optimized package imports in Next.js (Vercel engineering blog)
nodes.norm_label: how we optimized package imports in next.js (vercel engineering blog)
nodes.rationale: Describes the build-time barrel-import transform behind optimizePackageImports and its measured dev/build/cold-start gains.

nodes.label: Avoid Barrel File Imports
nodes.rationale: Barrel entry points can expose thousands of re-exports (up to 10,000), costing 200-800ms per cold start; importing from source files or letting Next.js rewrite barrel imports at build time gives 15-70% faster dev boot, 28% faster builds and 40% faster cold starts.

nodes.label: localStorage error handling
nodes.rationale: getItem and setItem throw in incognito/private browsing (Safari, Firefox), when quota is exceeded, or when storage is disabled, so every access needs a try/catch.

nodes.label: Version and Minimize localStorage Data
nodes.rationale: Version-prefixed keys make schema evolution explicit and prevent conflicts, storing only the fields the UI needs avoids persisting tokens, PII and internal flags, and try/catch is mandatory because storage APIs throw in private browsing or on quota errors.

nodes.label: Avoid Boolean Prop Proliferation
nodes.rationale: Each boolean prop doubles the possible states of a component, so flags like isThread/isEditing/isDMThread produce exponential conditional logic. Composition keeps every variant explicit about what it renders while still sharing internals.

nodes.label: Use Compound Components
nodes.rationale: Subcomponents read shared state from context rather than props, so consumers compose only the pieces they need with no hidden conditionals, and state/actions/meta are dependency-injected by a parent provider for multiple usages.

nodes.label: Prefer Composing Children Over Render Props
nodes.norm_label: prefer composing children over render props
nodes.rationale: Children are more readable and compose naturally without decoding callback signatures. Render props remain the right tool only when the parent must pass data or state down to the child, while children are for composing static structure.

nodes.label: Create Explicit Component Variants
nodes.rationale: Explicit variants (ThreadComposer, EditMessageComposer) document themselves: each declares its provider/state, its UI elements and its actions, so there are no boolean prop combinations to reason about and no impossible states.

nodes.label: React 19 API Changes (no forwardRef, use() over useContext())
nodes.norm_label: react 19 api changes (no forwardref, use() over usecontext())
nodes.rationale: In React 19 ref is a regular prop so the forwardRef wrapper is dead weight, and use() replaces useContext() with the added benefit that it can be called conditionally. The rule is React 19+ only and should be skipped on React 18 or earlier.

nodes.label: Define Generic Context Interfaces for Dependency Injection
nodes.norm_label: define generic context interfaces for dependency injection
nodes.rationale: A state/actions/meta interface is a contract any provider can implement, so the same UI components work against local useState, global Zustand, or server-synced state. UI consumes the interface, never the implementation, which makes state dependency-injectable.

nodes.label: Decouple State Management from UI
nodes.rationale: The provider should be the only place that knows how state is managed, so a state backend (useState, Zustand, server sync) can be swapped without touching the UI. Two providers with different backends drive the exact same composed UI.

nodes.label: Lift State into Provider Components
nodes.rationale: Lifting state into a provider lets sibling components outside the main UI read and modify it without prop drilling, useEffect syncing or reading state from a ref on submit. The provider boundary, not visual nesting, defines who can access shared state.

nodes.label: Combine Multiple Array Iterations
nodes.rationale: Multiple .filter() or .map() calls iterate the array multiple times; combining them into one loop reduces the number of iterations.

nodes.label: Use flatMap to Map and Filter in One Pass
nodes.norm_label: use flatmap to map and filter in one pass
nodes.rationale: Chaining .map().filter(Boolean) creates an intermediate array and iterates twice; .flatMap() transforms and filters in a single pass with no intermediate array.

nodes.label: Early Return from Functions
nodes.rationale: Returning as soon as the result is determined skips unnecessary processing; the incorrect version keeps scanning all items after the first error is found.

nodes.label: Early Length Check for Array Comparisons
nodes.norm_label: early length check for array comparisons
nodes.rationale: When comparing arrays with expensive operations (sorting, joining, deep equality) a length comparison is O(1) and proves inequality, so the costly work is skipped whenever lengths differ.

nodes.label: Use Lazy State Initialization
nodes.rationale: Passing a function to useState defers the initializer to the first render only. Without the function form, expensive initializers (index building, JSON parsing of localStorage, DOM reads) are recomputed on every render even though the value is used once.

nodes.label: Use after() for Non-Blocking Operations
nodes.rationale: Scheduling logging, analytics, notifications, cache invalidation and cleanup with after() lets the response be sent immediately while the side effect runs in the background. after() still runs when the response fails or redirects.

nodes.label: Build Index Maps for Repeated Lookups
nodes.norm_label: build index maps for repeated lookups
nodes.rationale: Repeated .find() calls by the same key are O(n) per lookup; building the Map once is O(n) and makes every subsequent lookup O(1) (1M ops reduced to 2K ops for 1000 orders x 1000 users).

nodes.label: Use Set/Map for O(1) Lookups
nodes.rationale: Array.includes is O(n) per membership check; converting the array to a Set or Map makes every lookup O(1).

nodes.label: Use Loop for Min/Max Instead of Sort
nodes.norm_label: use loop for min/max instead of sort
nodes.rationale: Finding the smallest or largest element only requires a single pass; sorting the whole array is O(n log n) and wasteful when only min/max are needed.

nodes.label: Math.min/Math.max Spread Alternative
nodes.rationale: Math.min/Math.max with spread is fine for small arrays but can be slower or throw for very large arrays due to spread operator argument limits, so the explicit loop is more reliable.

nodes.label: Immutable Array Methods (toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with)
nodes.norm_label: immutable array methods (tosorted, toreversed, tospliced, with)

nodes.label: Use toSorted() Instead of sort() for Immutability
nodes.norm_label: use tosorted() instead of sort() for immutability
nodes.rationale: .sort() mutates the array in place, which breaks React's immutability model for props and state and causes stale closure bugs; .toSorted() returns a new sorted array without mutation.

nodes.label: React Props/State Immutability Model
nodes.rationale: React expects props and state to be treated as read-only, so in-place mutation of a prop array both violates the model and produces stale closures when done inside callbacks or effects.

nodes.label: Use defer or async on Script Tags
nodes.norm_label: use defer or async on script tags
nodes.rationale: Script tags without defer or async block HTML parsing while downloading and executing, delaying First Contentful Paint and Time to Interactive; defer preserves execution order for DOM-dependent scripts while async suits independent scripts such as analytics.

nodes.label: Rendering Performance
nodes.rationale: Optimizing the rendering process reduces the work the browser needs to do.

nodes.label: Re-render Optimization
nodes.rationale: Reducing unnecessary re-renders minimizes wasted computation and improves UI responsiveness.

nodes.label: Server-Side Performance
nodes.rationale: Optimizing server-side rendering and data fetching eliminates server-side waterfalls and reduces response times.

nodes.label: React Best Practices Section Catalog
nodes.rationale: Defines the eight rule sections with their ordering and impact levels (CRITICAL down to LOW); the section ID is the filename prefix used to group rule files, so agents apply the highest-leverage rules first.

nodes.label: CSS content-visibility for Long Lists
nodes.rationale: content-visibility: auto defers off-screen layout and paint; for a 1000-message list the browser skips roughly 990 off-screen items, giving about a 10x faster initial render.

nodes.label: Subscribe to Derived State
nodes.rationale: Subscribing to a derived boolean (isMobile) instead of a continuous value (window width) means the component re-renders only when the boolean flips rather than on every pixel change.

nodes.label: Expo Versioned Docs Requirement (AGENTS.md)
nodes.rationale: Expo HAS CHANGED: SDK APIs evolve between releases, so the exact versioned documentation must be read before any code is written instead of relying on remembered API shapes.

nodes.label: Ship the Exact Build
nodes.rationale: The explicit build ID is used when multiple builds exist and an eligible uploaded build is reused for production only when its release code, icon, configuration and version already match; a successful upload does not create tester access or release the app publicly, and TestFlight distribution alone does not authorize a public release.
